before: I struck with the word, so that those being restored by it might correct themselves, and those disobedient to the word might be reproved, while those needing a separation by deeds [are identified].

Knowing that some are being persuaded even while hearing, I do not wish to use separation yet; rather, when those obeying appear, it may be shown who are being instructed by the word and who are in need of a turning back. Test accurately each one according to the worthiness of the face's conduct (2 Cor 10:7). This he sees regarding the apostles; for since it was  destined to reprove those from circumcision, and they were putting forward Peter and James and John, be certain, he says, lest the status of faces might ever prevent you from perceiving the truth. We write these things not imitating those commending themselves—for this is not good (2 Cor 10:12)—for they do not perceive that they themselves measure  themselves within themselves and are not able to compare themselves to another; for when compared to others they are nothing. We do not boast beyond our measure as if we were superior to greater things (2 Cor 10:14); for even unto you we came and proclaimed the word (2 Cor 10:15–16). They boast of their own labors regarding our things,  but we do not, but according to law we boast of the rule and the measure allotted to us, hoping to evangelize even beyond you as your faith increases. And he says 'rule' to mean reaching as far as them (2 Cor 10:17). Even if we boast, it is not as if we were rectifying by our own wisdom, but by the grace of the Spirit (2 Cor 11:2). You died, he says, to the law, and have become another  man, to the one risen from the dead. How then could a pure virgin have been previously married? But having been reborn through the bath of regeneration and having passed into another life, a pure virgin is justly so named. Faith in Christ and the brightness of the Spirit confirm the Christian life (2 Cor 11:4). If then you did not receive these things, you seek well those who still wish to live according to the law (2 Cor 11:10–12). Not reproaching the Corinthians, he says this, but  reproving those who use the preaching as a matter of commerce. Therefore he says that I do not stop boasting.

He means that I have not made the preaching a commercial venture like those; for I neither received anything from you nor do I receive, not as one not loving you—for I do love—but so that I might cut off the pretext of the accusers, so that whether they boast falsely or truly, they may be revealed just as we also are revealed (2 Cor 12:2–5).

To show this a strong, immortal soul; for if he had known it was mortal, he would not have been wavering whether he saw the vision outside the body or in the body. And regarding the third heaven, he said the third of the expanse; for if he had ascended up to the three heavens, he certainly would have heard the unspeakable words there and not in Paradise. And let no one suppose Paradise to be above the heaven; for according to the east it is planted upon the earth in the place of Eden, whence also Adam was formed, as Moses recounts. And he speaks of persecutions as weaknesses, not a bodily passion as some suppose (2 Cor 12:7).

It is suspected by many as having a pain around the head, but the truth is he speaks of persecutions, since the temptations came from a diabolical energy. And he called the one serving the temptation to the devil a Satanic angel, from a transformation of the angels serving God. And that which was given according to the forgiveness of God should be understood as also regarding Job; for God does not give evil (2 Cor 12:9).

You have an apostolic grace; do not seek this and succeed even without temptations; for my power is perfected in persecutions and tribulations (2 Cor 12:13). If then you have nothing to accuse me of, that I, having desisted from seeking sustenance despite the need, received nothing from you, in which even if you think I have sinned, forgive me and grant me grace for this injustice which you think is being done by me (2 Cor 12:14).

This testifies to them regarding the second and third time to be toward them because of the preaching (2 Cor 13:4). Just as Christ was said to have become sin and a curse, being neither sin nor a curse, but he took upon himself our evils so that we might be delivered from them; so also now, he is said to have been crucified not from his own weakness, but from that which he received on our behalf, the dispensations on our behalf.

before: It is said: he who seeks his own glory is not true, but he who seeks the glory of the one who sent him, he is true. If we were proclaiming ourselves, it would be suspected that we are deceiving with the word, but if we proclaim Christ and his glory, there is no deception in the preaching.

In the face of Jesus Christ (2 Cor 4:6), instead of 'through Jesus Christ', through him. Toward the illumination of knowledge, that the knowledge was not found by reasoning, but was revealed through revelation. Instead of 'through Jesus Christ' it shone in our hearts, and the knowledge was not found by reasoning, but was made known through revelation and illumination; for no man could ever reach this, having taken on flesh (2 Cor 4:7–9).

Through these and the following, he shows that God does not allow to be tested beyond what we are able. For even if we are being afflicted by those who persecute, yet we are not so distressed as to have no escape or recourse anywhere; for God widens the way for those afflicted through piety, as David says: 'In affliction you widened me' (2 Cor 4:10).

We always carry the death, always risking because, being partakers of the sufferings of Christ, we are [at risk] (2 Cor 4:11). The Lord was delivered unto death for us, but we for ourselves through Jesus, so that we might become partakers of his life (2 Cor 4:12).

Because of the preaching the apostles were risking, but they proclaimed so that the believing ones might live, and this is the life in you (2 Cor 4:13). Since, he says, there is a spirit of slavery in the law, but a spirit of adoption in the grace. And he said that we have the same spirit which David also had; the same spirit added the faith, not of the legal slavery. Having, he says, the same spirit as David who spoke according to faith, just as he said: 'I believed, therefore I spoke' (Psalm 116:5). Then, having said 'the spirit added the faith', for this is common to new and old only, since in the law there was a spirit of slavery, but in the grace a spirit of adoption.

If deaths and dangers and temptations follow (2 Cor 4:17–18), how is the affliction lighter? How is it being spent away? For the temptations remained with him and were driving him into old age. How then is the affliction of the saints light? Or is it evident that, being weighed against the glory of the coming age and against the prepared good things for the righteous, even the heaviest temptations appear light to me? And the afflictions are not merely light, but excessive, yet these afflictions fall far short of the greatness of the glory; for the great thing is a body and is heavy. Or he said 'weight' by way of a metaphor of the scales; for the glory, being weighed against the afflictions, is found to be most heavy of all. And he says 'spent away' regarding the temporal; for even if the crushing is long and causes grief, it appears temporal as compared to the infinite glory.

A dwelling, a tent; not the tent but the dwelling (2 Cor 5:1–2); for the dwelling here ceases, but the tent rises up. And he said 'dwelling' for the conduct, both the mortal and the expected. Furthermore, he shows that he calls the corruption and the incorruption 'dwellings'. He says 'dwelling, tent' regarding the body, which, he says, even if it should be corrupted in temptations and dangers through Christ, we shall lay it aside as a corruptible dwelling among the last of things made by hands. But we shall find in the heavens another dwelling, which God provides, incorruptible and not made by hands. Through these things, he shows both the mortal conduct and the immortal. Through the 'putting on', he shows that the corruptible flesh rises up and puts on the immortal; for the 'putting on' is said in reference to another garment. And he says 'two dwellings', the mortal and the expected; and 'two habitations', the corruption and the incorruption, because we are being laid aside from the one and are putting on the other. And he calls the one from heaven 'habitation'—the incorruption from the heavens—since it is not made by hands but is a gift of God. All indeed are righteous and unrighteous (2 Cor 5:3)...

Having said 'do not be compressed in us', he teaches this: instead of 'we do not compress you with the saving teaching, nor shall there be a lack from us'; for our heart has been widened and our mouth has been opened for teaching (2 Cor 6:11-13). before: God: the matter of deciding through God to come about is not a light thing. Having decided to come to you, I promised this not out of recklessness or carelessness; for not according to the flesh do I decide, but spiritually. It is proper that one deciding concerning spiritual things should nowhere be false, so that his yes may be yes and his no, no.

Indeed, whether it is to come or not to come is not in me, but the setting forth in me (2 Cor 1:18). If, therefore, the proclamation had yes and no, my decision    regarding my arrival to you would justly have yes and no; but if the word is true, then the whole decision is true. I believe to God that none of those things which we preached is a lie (2 Cor 1:19). For even the Son of God, our Lord Jesus, did not become a liar (2 Cor 1:19). Through Christ we send up the amen to God the Father,  the confirmation toward Christ we received through God; and through the one having sealed us, He demonstrated our belonging to God and our separation from the evil one (2 Cor 1:20–22). For even shepherds place their own seal upon the    flocks, distinguishing them from the strangers. Having said 'earnest', He presented that we have received a small deposit of the knowledge, but the perfection is owed to us; for the earnest is a part of the whole.

Because there were many complaints against them, he did not want, having gone, to condemn them (2 Cor 1:23–24). The word is spoken incompletely; for he wants to    say that I desired to come to you, but not as one who is lord and teacher of your faith. To correct those among you who stumble, and those among us who stumble, so that we might become fellow-workers of the joy according to God. To believe in you, and in us the correcting of those stumbling, so that we might become fellow-workers of the grace of God. And he says 'joy according to God'; for the apostle would not have joined in with them for a worldly joy. Having spoken of faith, he presented that they are left without works. Therefore, since they have faith as unfruitful and still incomplete, he says he is a fellow-worker to them.

Because of this I did not come, not so that I might not grieve you but myself, and so that I might not condemn anyone on account of what they are doing (2 Cor 2:1). You do not grieve me from those who are alike, and I    you; for you grieve me from those from whom you sin, but I grieve you from those whom I strike (2 Cor 2:2). But rejoice...

He appears to be feeling sorrow—for he who has not been grieved clearly shows that he did not even take heed when rebuked (2 Cor 2:3). For even if I grieve you, I am doing a proper thing;    cooperate toward my joy regarding your own benefit.

I wrote this, that sparing you, I did not come, so that at the end of this letter, where it lies, lest having come, God might humble me (2 Cor 2:4). And because of this I wrote, so that in gladness I might    find you having been corrected, so that you might not grieve. Not looking to my own, but to yours I said this; for I know that if you see me rejoicing, you rejoice, and if you see me grieving, you grieve. I wrote these things so that if you wish for me to come to you, you might beforehand correct the faults.

Showing that he makes the same faults his own, he brought grief and tears, which he has love toward them (2 Cor 2:5). Having said, I wrote to you, not that you might simply    be grieved, but that the joy according to God might take away the grief.

If anyone has grieved even him whom you love, he has not grieved me alone, but in part also you, so that I might not burden [you] by saying even Christ (2 Cor 2:6). And he fell silent from saying 'and Christ,' so that    he might not burden [you] even by saying it.

He says 'reproof' is the condemnation from the many (2 Cor 2:7). To forgive him this (2 Kor 2:8). Obey me in condemning, obey me also in recalling him who has been condemned (2 Cor 2:9). Forgive him this, he says; for you know that of those ch you forgive to this [man], I also desire to forgive (2 Kor 2:10). And because of this he shows that he wants them to think the same things about themselves by a disposition toward them.

He appears to have been grieved toward those in Troas, because they did not do much regarding Titus, nor did they hold him until his arrival, but as if they had become lawless concerning the faith, they departed (2 Cor 2:12-13). Thus, admonishing them as unworthy, he departed even    though a door had been opened and no one was closing against the proclamation. Or indeed because of this he departed, as being able easily to correct the things there later upon arrival, as no one being there to hinder.

This is to the one proclaiming our insults and the circumstances through Christ (2 Cor 2:14). But he confesses a greater grace regarding those things    through which he is made worthy to triumph through Christ. And he says these things also because of the Corinthians; for it was feared lest they might perhaps slay [him] because of the things...

before: I struck with the word, so that those being restored by it might correct themselves, and those disobedient to the word might be reproved, while those needing a separation by deeds [are identified].

Knowing that some are being persuaded even while hearing, I do not wish to use separation yet; rather, when those obeying appear, it may be shown who are being instructed by the word and who are in need of a turning back. Test accurately each one according to the worthiness of the face's conduct (2 Cor 10:7). This he sees regarding the apostles; for since it was  destined to reprove those from circumcision, and they were putting forward Peter and James and John, be certain, he says, lest the status of faces might ever prevent you from perceiving the truth. They boast of their own labors regarding our things,  but we do not, but according to law we boast of the rule and the measure allotted to us, hoping to evangelize even beyond you as your faith increases. And he says 'rule' to mean reaching as far as them (2 Cor 10:17). Even if we boast, it is not as if we were rectifying by our own wisdom, but by the grace of the Spirit (2 Corinthians 10:17). You died, he says, to the law, and have become another  man, to the one risen from the dead. How then could a pure virgin have been previously married? But having been reborn through the bath of regeneration and having passed into another life, a pure virgin is justly so named. Faith in Christ and the brightness of the Spirit confirm the Christian life (2 Cor 11:4). If then you did not receive these things, you seek well those who still wish to live according to the law (2 Cor 11:10–12). Not reproaching the Corinthians, he says this, but  reproving those who use the preaching as a matter of commerce. Therefore he says that I do not stop boasting.

This testifies to them regarding the second and third time to be toward them because of the preaching (2 Cor 13:4).
